Title: Why Your Eye Suddenly Looks Like It's Bleeding (It's Usually Fine)

Description:
A subconjunctival hemorrhage is a broken blood vessel under the clear surface of your eye - most people notice it in the mirror, not from any pain. It's often caused by the Valsalva effect: sudden pressure from coughing, sneezing, vomiting, heavy lifting, or straining. Rubbing your eyes and pressing hard on contact lenses can do the same thing, and aspirin or blood thinners make it bleed more and clear more slowly.

A cold compress for the first 10-15 minutes helps, then switch to warm after a few days. Use acetaminophen instead of aspirin for discomfort, and never stop a prescribed blood thinner on your own. Most cases clear up in one to three weeks - see a doctor if you notice pain, vision changes, or this keeps happening.

Caught a bright red patch on your eye in the mirror? 😳

That's a subconjunctival hemorrhage - usually just the Valsalva effect at work (coughing, sneezing, straining, heavy lifting) or a bit too much eye-rubbing. No pain, no vision change, just an alarming look.

Cold compress first, then warm after a few days - most cases clear up in one to three weeks on their own. On aspirin or blood thinners? Don't stop them without asking your doctor first.
